source.title: PTPP-Aware Adaptation Scaling Laws: Predicting Domain-Adaptation Performance at Unseen Pre-Training Budgets
source.authors: Étienne Goffinet; Shane Bergsma; Avraham Sheinin; N. Vassilieva; Shaheer Muhammad; Preslav Nakov; Gurpreet Gosal

record.file_problem: None; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests adaptation-loss forecasts at an unseen pre-training budget and refines the scaling-law account: its preferred formulation changes with domain and evaluation-stage anchoring.
record.gate_note: The paper reports aggregated forecast metrics for adaptation-loss scaling-law formulations and a D-CPT transfer baseline. These are aggregate results over the held-out evaluation grid, not individual loss values for each model, replay ratio, or adaptation-token budget. Figure 1 and Appendix C show curves but do not provide numeric point values in the text; those plotted values are not separately extracted.
record.test_reason: The study tests power-law-based loss models in continual pretraining, a new training regime relative to the originals. Held-out forecast errors bear on V5, and comparisons across domains, functional forms and anchoring conditions bear on the setup-dependence aspect of V7. It does not test orders-of-magnitude extrapolation from smaller models.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: PTPP-aware power-law-based adaptation models forecast French loss at an unseen pretraining stage, and the preferred functional form depends on domain and evaluation-stage supervision. The authors interpret this as pretraining progress affecting both the loss floor and adaptation efficiency. Their anchoring claims need qualification: French Form 3 MAErel worsens from 0.00670 to 0.00739, and Form 1 slope calibration worsens from 0.991 to 0.956, although Huber and RMSE improve.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits PTPP-aware continual-pretraining adaptation-loss formulas, rather than reproducing the original general pretraining scaling-law measurements. It evaluates forecasts across PTPP stages and uses a D-CPT transfer baseline.
record.method_sensitivity: Preferred formulation varies with domain and whether 20 small-scale evaluation-stage anchors are included. For the source domain, Form 1 is best without anchors and Form 2 with anchors; for French, Form 3 is best in both conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted-law optimization selects 8.9 adaptation tokens per parameter and 34% replay for an 8.1B model under forgetting and French-loss constraints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptation-loss models can guide replay and token-budget planning under constraints; this is a model-derived planning result, not a test of compute-optimal parameter/token scaling.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to GPT-2–style decoders in one English/Arabic-to-French setup, with fits at PTPP={15,31} and evaluation at PTPP=279. Results are aggregate metrics over evaluation grids; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors defer source-domain details to the appendix and note that uncertainty quantification remains future work.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numeric forecast metrics for the extracted conditions were left out. Figure 1 and Appendix C show plotted loss curves without numeric point values; the figure-only points were not extracted.

untested.parts: Ordinary held-out pretraining-loss scaling with non-bottleneck parameters, tokens or compute over several orders of magnitude.

Fits restricted to small runs predicting runs orders of magnitude larger. Training-stage extrapolation from PTPP 15 and 31 to 279 is approximately 9–19-fold, and fitting includes the evaluated model-size range.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its scaling exponents. Replay/token planning at fixed 8.1B size does not test this.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and adaptation settings beyond this English/Arabic-to-French setup; universality or uniqueness of the power-law form relative to alternative non-power-law models.
Downstream task performance; all measured outcomes are validation losses.

Numerical fitted-exponent comparisons, compute-optimal splits, parameter-counting or schedule effects, explanations of disagreements between published pretraining laws, and demonstrated departures from a single power law across extended scales.

missing.what: Calibration intercepts and RMSElog are omitted despite rows_left_out claiming no additional numeric forecast metrics were omitted. Intercepts are needed to interpret near-one slopes, and RMSE distinguishes anchoring improvements from the MAE worsening for French Form 3. French Form 1 intercept changes from -0.01 to 0.03; French Form 3 RMSElog improves from 0.00953 to 0.00842.

record.verdict_notes: All main numeric values match the supplied tables. These are aggregate forecast diagnostics, not individual observed loss curves or fitted exponents. V7 support is restricted to functional-form and calibration-data dependence. No uncertainty estimates or comparison against non-power-law alternatives are supplied; candidate-model rankings alone do not establish a unique underlying law.

versions.untested_parts: The study concerns continual-pretraining adaptation loss, not held-out pretraining loss as a function of model size, tokens, or compute when the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
It predicts at an unseen tokens-per-parameter stage, not loss for runs orders of magnitude larger in model size or compute than the fitting runs.
It optimizes adaptation tokens and replay ratio under constraints; it does not test how loss-minimizing parameter and token counts scale with pre-training compute.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests continual-pretraining adaptation in one multilingual source-to-target setup, not image/video modalities, repeated-data pretraining, fine-tuning generally, or transfer beyond the reported setup.
No downstream task performance evaluation; the measured outcomes are validation losses.
Compares candidate functional forms and evaluation-stage anchoring across two domains; does not report fitted exponents, a compute-optimal pretraining split, or curves bending away from a single law.

relationships.condition: French target loss at PTPP 279, with and without evaluation-stage anchors
relationships.reason: F0-M3 and F20-M3 report 0.670% and 0.739% relative forecast error for the gated-plus-floor power-law formulation, supporting its applicability to this adaptation regime.
relationships.display_finding: The gated power law with a loss floor forecast French loss with relative errors of 0.670% without evaluation anchors and 0.739% with anchors.

relationships.condition: Source-domain loss during adaptation, using the best formulation in each anchoring condition
relationships.reason: S0-M1 gives 1.18% relative error without anchors; S20-M2 gives 0.901% with anchors, supporting power-law-based modeling of source retention in this setting.
relationships.display_finding: The best power-law-based formulations forecast source-domain loss with relative errors of 1.18% without anchors and 0.901% with anchors.

relationships.condition: Applying the French-preferred gated-plus-floor formulation to source-domain loss without anchors
relationships.reason: S0-M3 gives 4.65% relative error versus 1.18% for Form 1 and 3.91% for D-CPT; predictive accuracy depends on the chosen formulation, although this does not reject power-law modeling generally.
relationships.display_finding: The gated-plus-floor formulation yielded 4.65% relative error, compared with 1.18% for Form 1 and 3.91% for D-CPT.

relationships.reason: F0-M3 is best for French at 0.670%, whereas S0-M1 is best for the source at 1.18%; these results support setup-dependent functional forms, without measuring numerical exponent changes.
relationships.display_finding: Without evaluation-stage anchors, different functional forms performed best for French and the source domain, with reported values of 0.670% and 1.18%, respectively.

relationships.condition: Source-domain fitting with versus without 20 evaluation-stage anchors
relationships.reason: S0-M1–S0-M3 favor Form 1 without anchors, while S20-M1–S20-M3 favor Form 2 with anchors; the preferred functional form depends on available calibration data.
relationships.display_finding: The preferred source-domain fit changed from Form 1 without anchors to Form 2 with 20 evaluation-stage anchors.

reader_labels.condition: French versus English/Arabic source domain, with and without 241M-scale evaluation-stage anchors
reader_labels.reason: The best-fitting formulation changes by domain and anchoring: Form 3 is best for French, while the source-domain preference changes from Form 1 without anchors to Form 2 with anchors (rows F0-H1–F0-S3, F20-H1–F20-S3, S0-H1–S0-S3, S20-H1–S20-S3).
